newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic's coalition headed for victory.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic's coalition headed for victory.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's leftist coalition said on Monday it had secured a parliamentary majority in federal elections after a campaign which promoted a new image of peacemaker.

Political commentators had predicted a comfortable victory for the coalition in Sunday's polls, the first in rump Yugoslavia since a four-year war in the Balkans, but were surprised at a strong showing by the ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party.

Ivica Dacic, spokesman for the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), told reporters the leftist coalition was assured of a majority in the federal parliament with two-thirds of the vote counted in Serbia and Montenegro, the two remaining Yugoslav republics.
Citing party estimates, Dacic said: "We expect the victory to be very convincing and that we will win an absolute majority...in the (federal) chamber of citizens."
With a firm grip on state media, police and finances, Milosevic's coalition had been expected to prevail.
Diplomats say Milosevic will probably assume the post of federal president after the next parliament invests the ceremonial post with strong executive authority.
The Radicals, who fell out with Milosevic over his decision to make concessions in peace negotiations, said they were pleased with their strong third place finish.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition won some 23 percent of the vote, the Radicals were close behind with about 18 percent, according to partial results.
Out of 2.2 million ballots counted, the leftist coalition had 1,093,234 votes, about 48 percent, the opposition coalition had 512,131 votes, and the Radicals had 406,967 votes.
The leftist coalition is comprised of the SPS, the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), led by Milosevic's powerful wife Mirjana Markovic, and New Democracy.

Analysts said the election results would enable Milosevic to portray himself to the West as a moderate alternative to the Radicals, who openly reject the U.S.-brokered peace treaty which ended war in Bosnia and Croatia a year ago.

In Montenegro, the Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS), allied with Milosevic's coalition, proclaimed victory in the republic's parliamentary elections, which coincided with the federal and municipal polls.
The ruling party won a majority of 45 seats in the 71-member parliament in Montenegro, the state news agency Tanjug reported, citing unofficial results.
Opposition parties, covering the political spectrum from liberal to right-wing nationalist, privately admitted defeat.
Opposition officials blamed the state-run media, a boycott by ethnic Albanians, lack of interest by the West and voter apathy for their poor performance.
But spokesmen for the opposition told a press conference he felt the results amounted to a victory considering a virtual media blockade imposed by state television and radio.
"The results are phenomenal considering the conditions," said Milan Paunovic of the Civic Alliance.
The opposition said it had won strong support at the local level and might win majorities in larger towns, including the capital, Belgrade.
The low voter turnout of 61 percent in Serbia and 67 percent in Montenegro, reported by the federal election commission, was bad news for the opposition.
Milosevic's coalition parties rely on loyal followers -- many of them pensioners -- with disciplined voting habits.
Ironically, Milosevic's foes in the predominantly Albanian province of Kosovo helped him cruise to victory.
The ethnic Albanian majority in Kosovo and fringe areas, accounting for 15 of 108 Serbian seats in the 138-seat federal parliament, helped Milosevic by boycotting the polls.

A team of election observers from the United States and several other states from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) monitored voting at some of the 10,000 polling stations.
Three election observers who attended the Socialist party press conference told reporters the elections were conducted under free and fair conditions with no major irregularities.
